entries.value: Built and shipped ClarityAtlas, an iOS health product, end to end in Swift and SwiftUI with a Supabase backend, as technical lead and co-founder of Open Health Intelligence. entries.label: Second example:
entries.value: A second example is ClarityAtlas, the iOS health product I co-founded Open Health Intelligence to build and serve as technical lead for. I built it end to end in Swift and SwiftUI with a Supabase backend, pulling from HealthKit and Core Motion. The hardest technical piece was estimating sleep without a wearable, so I built a passive estimation system on top of phone-interaction and motion signals like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns. I also built backend services for behavioral comparison, including a "Sleep Twins" matching system using standardized features and weighted distance. We shipped it into a live pilot at Johns Hopkins with 30+ users, and it was selected for the Pava Spark Accelerator and NSF I-Corps. What that project taught me is that building the system is only part of making something real. Recruiting users, sitting with their feedback, and explaining repeatedly why the thing should exist mattered as much as the code. That is the part I would want to carry into work where the product has to function for a specific person in their actual daily life.
entries.reason: Essay generated from the operator's about-me context

entries.label: Third example:
entries.value: I ran an independent research project on Valley Fever and environmental disease modeling. I built an SIR-style epidemiological model in Python starting from the differential equations rather than a packaged library, because I wanted to be able to change the compartment structure as I connected disease dynamics to environmental variables around dust and agriculture. I also programmed a microcontroller-based dust sensor in C/C++ so the environmental side of the model was tied to measurements I collected instead of only published data. The work became a sole-author publication in the Journal of Student Research and led to my selection as a national finalist in the Junior Science and Humanities Symposium. What mattered to me afterward was less the result than the shift in how I thought about modeling. Before this I treated math as a self-contained exercise; building the sensor and the model together made me care about whether a model explains something real.
